claim: NIH distributes over $34 billion per year in research grants to support biomedical research at research institutions and small businesses across the United States.
source: National Institutes of Health (NIH) distributes over $34 billion per year in research grants to support biomedical research at research institutions and small businesses across the United States.
evidence: This is a factual statement about NIH funding levels, presented as established knowledge without specific citation.

claim: In 2011, the National Academies of Science issued a report arguing that increased diversity in the scientific workforce is critical to ensure that the United States maintains its global leadership and competitive edge in science and technology.
source: In 2011, the National Academies of Science (NAS) issued a report arguing that increased diversity in the scientific workforce is critical to ensure that the United States maintains its global leadership and competitive edge in science and technology (National Academy of Sciences, N.A.o.E, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the National Academy of Sciences report from 2011.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006, the likelihood of Black PIs being awarded NIH research funding was 55% of that of White investigators.
source: The same year, Ginther et al. reported that the likelihood of Black PIs being awarded NIH research funding between 2000 and 2006 was 55% of that of White investigators (Ginther et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ginther et al., 2011.

claim: The funding gap between Black and White investigators persists.
source: This funding gap persists (Ginther et al., 2011; Ginther et al., 2018; Hoppe et al., 2019; Erosheva et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting the persistent funding gap.

claim: The proportion of NIH research grant applicants who are Black increased from 1.4% in Ginther's data to 2.3% in 2020.
source: the proportion of NIH research grant applicants who are Black has increased only slightly in the ensuing years, from 1.4% in Ginther's data to 2.3% in 2020.
evidence: This claim presents specific data comparing proportions across time periods, drawing from Ginther's data and 2020 data.

claim: The largest single factor determining the probability of funding in the highly competitive NIH system is the outcome of peer review.
source: The largest single factor determining the probability of funding in the highly competitive NIH system is the outcome of peer review.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the NIH funding system.

claim: Funding rates for major research grants vary approximately threefold, from about 10% to nearly 30%, across NIH institutes.
source: Funding rates for major research grants vary approximately threefold, from about (10% to nearly 30%) across the institutes meaning that applications in some areas of science enjoy greater success than others.
evidence: This claim presents specific data about funding rate variation across NIH institutes.

claim: The topics most often studied by Black investigators tend to have low funding rates.
source: A recent paper focused attention on the finding that funding success varied substantially depending on scientific topic, and that the topics most often studied by Black investigators tend to have low funding rates (Hoppe et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoppe et al., 2019.

claim: The association between topics studied by Black investigators and low funding rates was primarily attributable to the disparate funding rates across the 24 NIH institutes, rather than topical bias in peer review.
source: An important follow-up paper showed that this association was primarily attributable to the disparate funding rates across the 24 NIH institutes, rather than topical bias in peer review (Lauer et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lauer et al., 2021.

claim: Blinding reviewers to applicant identity and institutional affiliations has been proposed as an approach to reducing demographic bias in review.
source: Blinding reviewers (in 'double blind' or 'dual anonymous' reviews) to applicant identity and institutional affiliations is one such approach (Cox and Montgomerie, 2019; Fisher et al., 1994; Haffar et al., 2019; Okike et al., 2016; Snodgrass, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies discussing blinding as an approach.

claim: The literature examining the impact of blinding on review outcomes is mixed with respect to gender.
source: The literature examining the impact of blinding on review outcomes is mixed. With respect to gender, for example, blinding has been reported to reduce disparities (Budden et al., 2008; Terrell et al., 2017; Aloisi and Reid, 2019) but has also been ineffectual (Primack, 2009; Whittaker, 2008; Blank, 1991; Ledin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations showing both positive and null effects of blinding.

claim: There are no studies evaluating real review of scientific grants blinded with respect to race.
source: To our knowledge, there are no studies evaluating real review of scientific grants blinded with respect to race.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

source: An NIH Advisory Committee to the Director (ACD) Working Group on Diversity in the Biomedical Research Workforce (WGDBRW) recommended that 'NIH should design an experiment to determine the effects of anonymizing applications…' in peer review (Working Group on Diversity in the Biomedical Research Workforce (WGDBRW) and T.A.C.t.t.D. (ACD), 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Working Group report from 2012.
